_meta.notes: Comprehensive index for Hong Kong covering prehistoric Yuet/Baiyue settlements, Han-era inclusion in Nanyue, Song dynasty refugees, Portuguese contact 1514, Qing era, Opium War and Treaty of Nanking 1842 (Hong Kong Island ceded), Convention of Peking 1860 (Kowloon), New Territories lease 1898, Japanese occupation 1941-1945, post-war economic miracle, 1967 riots, handover to China 1997 (One Country Two Systems), 2014 Umbrella Movement, 2019 protests, and National Security Law 2020.

country_profile.capital: N/A (city-territory; Central is de facto centre)
country_profile.currency: Hong Kong dollar (HKD, pegged to USD)

ethnic_groups.name: Chinese (Cantonese)
ethnic_groups.notes: Predominantly Cantonese; also Hakka, Teochew, Shanghainese, Fujianese; post-1949 mainland refugees shaped modern HK

ethnic_groups.name: Filipino
ethnic_groups.notes: Largest non-Chinese group; domestic workers; ~200,000; Sunday gatherings in Central

ethnic_groups.name: South Asian (Indian, Pakistani, Nepali)
ethnic_groups.notes: Historical community since British era; Indian traders (Sindhi, Gujarati); Gurkha/Nepali community; Pakistani community

ethnic_groups.name: White/European
ethnic_groups.notes: British legacy; international business community; declining

ethnic_groups.name: Other
ethnic_groups.notes: Japanese, Korean, Thai, mixed heritage; Tanka (boat people, historically marginalised)

independence.notes: One Country Two Systems guaranteed until 2047; Basic Law is mini-constitution

country_profile.notes_unique: World's freest economy (Heritage Foundation, historically); highest Michelin-starred street food; world's most expensive real estate per sqft; Victoria Peak/harbour iconic skyline
country_profile.national_anthem: Yìyǒngjūn Jìnxíngqǔ (March of the Volunteers, PRC anthem)

geography.terrain: Hilly to mountainous; lowlands in north; 263 islands; extensive reclamation
geography.notes: Special Administrative Region of China; one of world's most densely populated places; Victoria Harbour iconic; 75% green/country park; land reclamation creates new territory.

economy_extended.poverty_line_definition: Government poverty line (50% median household income)
economy_extended.notes: World's freest economy (Heritage Foundation); global financial centre (#4); world's most expensive real estate; no sales tax; HKD pegged to USD (Linked Exchange Rate); re-export hub for China; extreme inequality (highest Gini in developed world).

health.notes: World's highest life expectancy (~85 years); dual public/private healthcare system; Doctor-Hong Kong shortage; world's first SARS outbreak 2003; COVID zero policy 2020-22.

food_agriculture.notes: 98% food imported (primarily from mainland China); agriculture <0.1% GDP; rooftop/vertical farming experiments; world-class food culture; Michelin-star density among world's highest.

energy.notes: 100% energy imported; 25% electricity from Daya Bay nuclear plant (Guangdong); phasing out coal for natural gas; offshore wind potential; CLP and HK Electric duopoly; world-class grid reliability.

transport.notes: MTR metro system world-class (99.9% on-time); Hong Kong International Airport (HKIA) among world's top cargo airports; Octopus card universal payment; Hong Kong-Zhuhai-Macau Bridge (55 km, world's longest sea crossing bridge); Star Ferry iconic.

tourism.notes: One of world's most visited cities; shopping/dining destination; Chinese mainland visitors dominant; post-COVID recovery; Star Ferry and Peak Tram iconic; Geopark volcanic formations.

legal_system.notes: One Country Two Systems (until 2047); National Security Law (2020) fundamentally changed legal landscape; Basic Law mini-constitution; once-independent judiciary facing Beijing pressure; Article 23 enacted 2024.

human_rights_gender.lgbtq_legal_status: Legal (no marriage/civil union; partial court victories)
human_rights_gender.notes: Dramatic decline in freedoms post-NSL 2020; Apple Daily shut down; pro-democracy activists imprisoned; media self-censorship; foreign domestic helpers (400k+) exploitation concerns; previously strong rule of law eroding.

security_stability.notes: Extremely low crime rate; PLA garrison present but rarely visible; 2019 pro-democracy protests (2M+ marchers); post-NSL political stability through suppression; no conventional security threats.

cultural_heritage.notes: Bruce Lee and kung fu cinema global impact; Cantopop golden era (1980s); East-meets-West cultural fusion; world capital of dim sum; M+ museum (Asia's largest modern art museum); comic book culture (manhua).

comparative_rankings.notes: World's freest economy and top financial centre; HDI among highest globally; sharp decline in freedom/press rankings post-2020; extreme housing unaffordability.
comparative_rankings._note: Country position relative to continent and global. 'rank' = 1 is best/largest.

current_leader.name: John Lee Ka-chiu
current_leader.title: Chief Executive
current_leader.notes: Pro-Beijing; former security secretary; sole candidate; US/UK sanctioned; National Security Law enforcer

former_chief_executives.name: Tung Chee-hwa
former_chief_executives.notes: First CE post-handover; Shanghai shipping magnate; unpopular; Article 23 controversy 2003; resigned

former_chief_executives.name: Donald Tsang
former_chief_executives.notes: Civil servant; knighted; later convicted of misconduct

former_chief_executives.name: Leung Chun-ying (CY Leung)
former_chief_executives.notes: Polarising; Occupy Central/Umbrella Movement 2014 on his watch

former_chief_executives.name: Carrie Lam
former_chief_executives.notes: Extradition bill triggered 2019 protests (largest in HK history); National Security Law June 2020; US sanctioned

last_british_governor.name: Chris Patten
last_british_governor.notes: Last Governor; democratic reforms; controversial with Beijing; emotional handover ceremony June 30, 1997

910.name: Prehistoric and Ancient Hong Kong
910.description: The archaeological evidence of Neolithic settlement in the Hong Kong region, the territory's role as a peripheral maritime zone of successive Chinese empires, and the salt and pearl industries.

sub_clusters.name: Neolithic and Bronze Age Settlement
sub_clusters.description: Archaeological sites on Lantau and Lamma Islands showing early habitation, geometric pottery, stone and bronze tool manufacture, and evidence of maritime trade connections.
key_events: Bronze Age rock carvings at sites across Hong Kong's islands — evidence of ancient ritual activity

sub_clusters.name: Imperial Chinese Periphery
sub_clusters.description: The Hong Kong region as part of Nanhai Commandery, the salt production industry, the flight of the last Song dynasty emperors through the area, the pearl diving industry, and the arrival of the Five Great Clans.
key_events: Last Song Emperor Bing dies at the naval Battle of Yamen near present-day Hong Kong (1279)
The Five Great Clans (Tang, Hau, Pang, Liu, Man) settle in the New Territories (from the 12th century)

920.name: Early European Contact and Qing Hong Kong
920.description: Portuguese and European traders along the South China coast, the Canton System of restricted trade, the opium trade, and the events leading to the British seizure of Hong Kong Island.

sub_clusters.name: Canton Trade System
sub_clusters.description: The Qing restriction of all Western trade to Canton, the cohong merchant monopoly, the growing British opium trade imbalance, Commissioner Lin Zexu's opium destruction, and the prelude to war.
key_events: Commissioner Lin Zexu confiscates and destroys over 20,000 chests of British opium at Canton (1839)

sub_clusters.name: First Opium War and Cession
sub_clusters.description: The First Opium War between Britain and the Qing Empire, Captain Charles Elliot's occupation of Hong Kong Island, and the Treaty of Nanjing permanently ceding Hong Kong to Britain.
key_events: British forces occupy Hong Kong Island (January 26, 1841)
Treaty of Nanjing — Hong Kong Island ceded to Britain 'in perpetuity' (August 29, 1842)

930.name: Victorian Colonial Hong Kong
930.description: The establishment and growth of the Crown Colony, the acquisition of Kowloon and the New Territories, the entrepôt trade, the plague, and Hong Kong's development as a gateway between China and the world.

sub_clusters.name: Crown Colony Establishment
sub_clusters.description: Governor Sir Henry Pottinger's administration, the development of Victoria City, the free port policy attracting trade, the Taiping refugees, and the Second Opium War leading to the acquisition of Kowloon.
key_events: Convention of Peking — Britain acquires Kowloon Peninsula and Stonecutters Island (1860)

sub_clusters.name: New Territories Lease and Plague
sub_clusters.description: The devastating bubonic plague of 1894 (where Alexandre Yersin identified the plague bacillus), the Convention for the Extension of Hong Kong Territory leasing the New Territories for 99 years, and the Six-Day War of 1899.
key_events: Alexandre Yersin identifies the plague bacillus in Hong Kong during the epidemic (1894)
Convention of Peking — New Territories leased to Britain for 99 years until 1997 (1898)

930.name: Early 20th Century Colonial Hong Kong
930.description: Hong Kong's growth as a regional hub, the 1925 Canton-Hong Kong Strike, the influx of refugees from China's upheavals, and the development of colonial society on the eve of the Japanese invasion.

sub_clusters.name: Strikes and Interwar Growth
sub_clusters.description: The 1922 Seamen's Strike, the devastating Canton-Hong Kong Strike and Boycott paralyzing the economy for 16 months, the growth of the financial sector, and interwar colonial society.
key_events: Canton-Hong Kong Strike and Boycott — 16-month labor action cripples the colony (1925–1926)

sub_clusters.name: Japanese Invasion and Occupation
sub_clusters.description: The Battle of Hong Kong and the British surrender on 'Black Christmas,' the brutal Japanese occupation with mass starvation and atrocities, the forced population reduction, and liberation.
key_events: Battle of Hong Kong — British garrison surrenders on Christmas Day (December 25, 1941)
Japanese occupation reduces Hong Kong's population from 1.6 million to 600,000 through deportation and starvation

940.name: Postwar Transformation
940.description: The resumption of British rule, the massive refugee influx from Communist China, the birth of Hong Kong's manufacturing industry, squatter fires, and the 1967 leftist riots.

sub_clusters.name: Refugee Influx and Industrialization
sub_clusters.description: The flood of refugees after the Chinese Communist victory, Shanghai industrialists bringing capital and expertise, the Shek Kip Mei fire and the birth of public housing, and the textile manufacturing boom.
key_events: Shek Kip Mei squatter fire leaves 53,000 homeless — launches Hong Kong's massive public housing program (1953)

sub_clusters.name: 1967 Leftist Riots
sub_clusters.description: The Star Ferry riots of 1966, the Cultural Revolution-inspired leftist riots of 1967 with bombings across the city, and the colonial government's crackdown that paradoxically catalyzed social reforms.
key_events: 1967 Leftist Riots — Cultural Revolution-inspired violence with over 800 bombs planted across Hong Kong

940.name: Economic Takeoff and Lion Rock Spirit
940.description: Hong Kong's transformation into one of the Four Asian Tigers, the ICAC anti-corruption drive, the development of a distinct Hong Kong identity, the 'Lion Rock Spirit' of self-reliance, and the Sino-British negotiations.

sub_clusters.name: Four Asian Tigers Era
sub_clusters.description: The rapid manufacturing-to-services transition, the rise of the property tycoons, Murray MacLehose's social reforms, the establishment of ICAC, and Hong Kong's emergence as a global financial center.
key_events: Independent Commission Against Corruption (ICAC) established — transforms Hong Kong governance (1974)

sub_clusters.name: Sino-British Negotiations
sub_clusters.description: Margaret Thatcher's visit to Beijing, Deng Xiaoping's insistence on sovereignty, the crisis of confidence and property crash, and the Sino-British Joint Declaration promising 'one country, two systems.'
key_events: Sino-British Joint Declaration signed — Hong Kong to return to China in 1997 under 'one country, two systems' (December 19, 1984)

950.name: Transition Era and Handover
950.description: The transitional period before the handover, the drafting of the Basic Law, the Tiananmen impact, Governor Patten's democratic reforms, emigration waves, and the 1997 handover ceremony.

sub_clusters.name: Basic Law and Tiananmen Impact
sub_clusters.description: The drafting of the Basic Law as Hong Kong's mini-constitution, the massive 1989 protest in support of Tiananmen demonstrators, the crisis of confidence, and the wave of emigration to Canada, Australia, and the UK.
key_events: One million Hong Kongers march in support of Tiananmen Square democracy protesters (May 1989)

sub_clusters.name: Patten Reforms and Handover
sub_clusters.description: Governor Chris Patten's controversial democratic reforms, Beijing's fury and creation of the Provisional Legislature, the new airport at Chek Lap Kok, and the handover ceremony in the rain at midnight on July 1, 1997.
key_events: Hong Kong handover ceremony — Prince Charles and Patten depart as the Union Jack is lowered (July 1, 1997)

950.name: Early SAR Period
950.description: The first years of the Hong Kong Special Administrative Region under Tung Chee-hwa, the Asian Financial Crisis, SARS, the massive Article 23 protests, and growing Beijing-Hong Kong tensions.

sub_clusters.name: Tung Administration and Crises
sub_clusters.description: The Asian Financial Crisis devastating the property market, the SARS epidemic, the July 1 2003 march of 500,000 against the Article 23 national security bill, and Tung Chee-hwa's resignation.
key_events: 500,000 march against the Article 23 national security bill — it is withdrawn (July 1, 2003)

sub_clusters.name: Growing Tensions with Beijing
sub_clusters.description: The NPCSC's ruling against universal suffrage, the rise of localist movements, anti-mainland sentiment, the national education controversy, and the buildup to the Umbrella Movement.
key_events: NPCSC decision restricts candidates for Chief Executive election — sparking outrage (August 2014)

960.name: Umbrella Movement to National Security Law
960.description: The Umbrella Movement, the 2019 anti-extradition protests, Beijing's imposition of the National Security Law, the transformation of Hong Kong's political landscape, and the emigration exodus.

sub_clusters.name: Umbrella Movement
sub_clusters.description: The 79-day Occupy Central / Umbrella Movement demanding genuine universal suffrage, the tear gas at Admiralty, the occupation of Mongkok and Causeway Bay, and the movement's ultimate failure to achieve democratic reform.
key_events: Umbrella Movement — pro-democracy protesters occupy major roads for 79 days (September–December 2014)

sub_clusters.name: 2019 Protests and National Security Law
sub_clusters.description: The massive anti-extradition bill protests with up to two million marchers, escalating violence, Beijing's imposition of the National Security Law, the crackdown on civil society and media, and the large-scale emigration wave.
key_events: An estimated two million march against the Extradition Bill (June 16, 2019)
Beijing imposes the National Security Law — fundamentally altering Hong Kong's political landscape (June 30, 2020)

unassigned_events.note: Events not yet assigned to a thematic cluster
